title: One Problem, Four Methods
oneLiner: Take one tiny driving problem whose answer we already know, hide the rulebook, and watch Monte Carlo, TD, SARSA and Q-learning learn it from experience.

what.html:
We reuse the race car (Cool/Warm/Overheated, drive Slow or Fast). Dynamic programming solved it with the full rulebook: fast when cool, slow when warm. Now the agent only gets to drive. Different methods learn from the same experience in different ways: wait until the drive ends and total the score (Monte Carlo), or update after every step using a guess about the next state (TD, SARSA, Q-learning).

Everyday versionLearning a commute: you can rate a route only after arriving (Monte Carlo), or adjust your estimate at every junction based on how far you think you still are (TD).

why.html:
• Same problem, same data: the only difference is the update rule, so you can see exactly what each rule does.
  • We know the right answer, so we can check who gets there.
  • These are the exact updates used inside deep RL.

how.title: The episode we'll reuse
how.html: Cool → fast (+2) → Warm → slow (+1) → Cool → fast (+2) → Warm → fast (−10) → overheated. Every method processes this same drive.

how.title: Monte Carlo: score the whole drive
how.html: Work backwards from the end: −10, then 2 + 0.6 × (−10) = −4, then −1.4, then 1.16. Each state–action pair gets the total that followed its first visit.

how.title: Learning from someone else's driving
how.html: Off-policy learning reweights experience: if the explorer chose Slow only 40% of the time but our target always would, that step counts 2.5×. If the explorer did something our target never would, the experience before it is discarded.

how.title: TD: update every step
how.html: After Cool → Warm with +2: new V(Cool) = 0 + 0.5 × (2 + 0.9 × 0 − 0) = 1. After Warm → Cool with +1: V(Warm) = 0.5 × (1 + 0.9 × 1) = 0.95. No need to wait for the end.

how.title: SARSA: learn the policy you follow
how.html: Update Q for the action taken using the next action you actually take. It learns how good your exploring habits are, risks included, so it values everything a bit lower and plays safer.

how.title: Average or best next action
how.html: Expected SARSA averages the next action's values (less noise). Q-learning uses the best next action, even if you didn't take it, so it learns the optimal values while still exploring.

how.title: Don't trust the luckiest number
how.html: Taking the maximum of noisy estimates is too optimistic. Double Q-learning keeps two tables: one picks the best action, the other says how good it is.

demo.html: Let three methods drive thousands of episodes. Q-learning heads for the optimal 15.5; SARSA and Monte Carlo settle near 11, the value of driving with occasional random choices.

example.html:
Same first step, different later steps. With all values at 0, SARSA, Expected SARSA and Q-learning all set Q(Cool, Fast) to 0.8 × 2 = 1.6. They only disagree once the next state's actions have different values: if Q(Warm, Slow) = 0 and Q(Warm, Fast) = 5, Q-learning uses 5, SARSA uses whichever was taken, and Double Q uses the other table's opinion of the chosen action.

Supplementary The different answers aren't errors: on-policy methods answer "how good is my actual behaviour?", off-policy ones "how good could it be?"

misunderstandings: SARSA and Q-learning learn the same values.
SARSA learns the exploring policy's values; Q-learning learns q*.
It needs the full return, so it waits.
It uses the observed reward and next state only.
Max of noisy estimates is biased upward.
takeaways: Same race car, same episode, different update rules.
MC: full returns, no bootstrapping, high variance.
TD(0), SARSA, Expected SARSA, Q-learning bootstrap every step.
Off-policy learning reweights by π/b; Q-learning uses max.
Double Q fixes maximisation bias; DP/MC/TD differ only in evaluation.
thirty: On the race car (v* = (15.5, 14.5)), one episode C,F,+2,W,S,+1,C,F,+2,W,F,−10,O illustrates every method. Monte Carlo (γ = 0.6) computes returns 1.16, −1.4, −4, −10 and assigns first-visit values. Off-policy MC reweights by π/b (1/0.4 = 2.5; zero once the behaviour deviates). TD(0) (γ = 0.9, α = 0.5) updates during the episode to V(C) = 1, V(W) = 0.95. SARSA (α = 0.8) gives Q(C,F) = 1.6, Q(W,S) = 1.952, Q(W,F) = −8; Expected SARSA averages next actions; Q-learning bootstraps from the max (17.15 after a +20 reward) and learns q*, while on-policy methods learn the ε-greedy policy's values (~11). Double Q-learning (5.2 in the worked step) removes maximisation bias. DP needs the model; MC waits for episode ends with high variance; TD bootstraps every step.

check.q: γ = 0.6, last two rewards 2 then −10. G for the step with reward 2?
TD(0), α = 0.5, γ = 0.9: V(W) after W→C (+1) with V(C) = 1?
Which method learns q* while behaving ε-greedily?
